epidermal-growth-factor-egf.summary: A growth-factor protein added to skincare serums to speed skin renewal and smooth the look of wrinkles.

quick.overview:
Epidermal growth factor (EGF) is a natural protein that tells skin cells to grow and repair. Serums with EGF are used by people who want smoother, younger-looking skin and softer wrinkles.

EGF binds receptors on skin cells, which drives cell turnover and repair. Its discoverers won a Nobel Prize, and a recombinant form is used medically for diabetic foot ulcers. For facial skin aging, one small serum trial has been registered, with no published results.
quick.how: People use EGF as a cosmetic serum applied to the face, usually in a regular morning or evening routine alongside moisturiser and sunscreen. It is often grouped with other growth-factor and peptide skincare ingredients. Skin-texture changes from this kind of product are typically judged over weeks of consistent use.
quick.risks: Safety of medical EGF is described as poorly studied, and EGF signalling is a research focus in cancer biology. No study found has tested cosmetic EGF for cancer risk. Serums vary in formulation and as cosmetics are not held to drug-style approval.

angle.text: EGF serums aim at smoother, younger-looking skin: the protein binds skin cell receptors, which increases cell turnover and repair. The biology of EGF is well described, and one small serum trial for skin aging has been registered.

cjc-ipa-protocol.summary: A pairing of two growth-hormone-releasing peptides that forum users take for muscle, leanness and recovery; neither part is an approved drug.

quick.overview:
CJC/IPA combines CJC-1295 with ipamorelin, two peptides that prompt the body to release more growth hormone. People use it hoping for more muscle, a leaner look and faster recovery.

CJC-1295 mimics growth-hormone-releasing hormone and ipamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor; together they raise growth hormone and IGF-1, which feed recovery, muscle and fat metabolism. No trial has tested the pair for appearance. The two were studied separately: CJC-1295 reached phase II before research stopped, and ipamorelin did not pass a phase II trial for postoperative ileus.
quick.how: It is discussed in forums and peptide circles as a stack that users buy as research peptides and run for body-composition goals alongside training and diet. Users describe changes in recovery and body composition building over weeks to months.
quick.risks: CJC-1295 research was stopped after a participant died, which the physician attributed to unrelated coronary disease. Users report water retention, including in the face and around the eyes, and forum threads ask about effects in teenagers' growth plates. Neither compound is approved, both are sold as research peptides, and both are on the WADA prohibited list.

angle.text: CJC/IPA raises growth hormone release, which raises IGF-1 and supports recovery, so users aim for more muscle and a leaner look. Forum users also mention water retention changing the face and eyes; the pair has not been tested in a trial.

tesa-ipa-protocol.summary: A tesamorelin plus ipamorelin peptide stack used in body-composition circles to cut belly fat and get leaner.

quick.overview:
Tesa/IPA stacks two growth-hormone-axis peptides, tesamorelin and ipamorelin, and is used for fat loss, especially around the midsection, and a leaner look.

Tesamorelin mimics growth-hormone-releasing hormone and ipamorelin acts on the ghrelin receptor, so both raise growth hormone and IGF-1 through different routes. Tesamorelin is a prescription drug approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, where trials looked at visceral fat. Ipamorelin was developed for postoperative ileus and dropped. No trial has tested the combination.
quick.how: In peptide circles the stack is run alongside diet and training for body composition, with fat-loss changes described over weeks to months. Tesamorelin is prescription-only and ipamorelin is typically sold as a research peptide.
quick.risks: Tesamorelin effects reported in its use include injection-site reactions, edema, joint pain and glucose intolerance. Ipamorelin is unapproved and on the WADA prohibited list. The combination has no safety data.

angle.text: Tesa/IPA aims at a leaner midsection: both peptides raise growth hormone, which is linked to less visceral fat. Tesamorelin has trial data for visceral fat in a specific patient group; the combination has not been trialled.

gt20029.summary: An experimental topical gel that breaks down the androgen receptor in scalp skin, being developed for male pattern hair loss.

quick.overview:
GT20029 is an investigational topical treatment for male pattern hair loss that aims to slow loss and bring back density without a pill. Interest centres on it as a possible alternative to finasteride-type drugs.

It is a PROTAC: it tags the androgen receptor for destruction in scalp skin, so DHT has less to act on in follicles, and being topical aims to keep it local. Phase 1 safety trials were completed and a Phase 2 trial in 180 Chinese men has been published.
quick.how: It is not available as a regulated product, so use is limited to people following trial news. In the Phase 2 trial it was applied to the scalp as a topical.
quick.risks: Phase 1 and 2 safety data exist but detailed long-term data do not. It is not approved anywhere, and the trials were early-phase, mainly in Chinese men.

angle.text: GT20029 aims at slower hair loss and more hair by breaking down the androgen receptor in scalp skin, so DHT has less effect on follicles, without exposing the whole body. A Phase 2 trial in 180 men has been published; it is not approved.

liposomal-igf-1.summary: IGF-1 packaged in fat-like carriers for the scalp, aimed at thicker hair by extending the follicle growth phase.

quick.overview:
Liposomal IGF-1 is a topical idea for thicker scalp hair: deliver the growth factor IGF-1 to hair follicles inside fat-like carriers.

IGF-1 is made naturally by follicle cells, and a 2025 review reports that it stimulates follicle proliferation and blood vessel growth and extends the growth phase through PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signalling. The supporting work is laboratory and animal research; no human hair-loss trial of a topical liposomal form was found.
quick.how: It is discussed in hair-loss communities as a scalp product applied topically, often next to established hair treatments. Hair changes are generally judged over several months.
quick.risks: Safety of topical IGF-1 on the scalp has not been established in published trials. It is an unapproved product for hair.

angle.text: Liposomal IGF-1 is meant to carry IGF-1 to the follicle, extend the growth phase and give thicker scalp hair. In lab work IGF-1 promotes follicle proliferation; human trials of the topical form have not been found.

hedgehog-pathway-agonist.summary: A class of topical compounds that switched on Hedgehog signalling to move follicles into growth for hair regrowth; development reportedly ended.

quick.overview:
Hedgehog pathway agonists were explored as topical hair-growth drugs to bring dormant follicles back to producing hair.

The Hedgehog pathway is reported to be required for follicles to move from rest into the growth phase, and agonists activate it through Smoothened and GLI signalling, the opposite of anticancer Smoothened inhibitors such as vismodegib. One program is associated in community discussion with Curis and Procter & Gamble. No human efficacy results were found.
quick.how: No product is available, so there is no routine to follow. It is followed in hair-loss discussion as a past research direction.
quick.risks: According to Wikipedia, the hair-growth effort failed because of toxicities found in animal models. Activating this pathway is a concern in tissue-growth contexts in general.

angle.text: Hedgehog agonists were developed to switch on the signalling that moves follicles from rest into the growth phase, aiming at hair regrowth. The effort was reportedly discontinued over animal toxicity, and no product is available.

adenosine-topical-hair.summary: A cosmetic hair-growth ingredient that acts on dermal papilla cells to extend the growth phase for thicker-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Topical adenosine is an ingredient in hair-growth cosmetics, used by people hoping to thicken thinning hair.

It acts on dermal papilla cells, the follicle's signalling centre: a 2012 study in cultured mouse whisker follicles found it raised FGF-2 and FGF-7, stimulated dermal papilla growth and lengthened the growth phase. A 2024 paper found the androgen receptor pathway to be a candidate target, separate from minoxidil's mechanism. The work is laboratory-based.
quick.how: It is applied to the scalp as a leave-on serum or tonic in a daily routine, and is sometimes used next to other hair treatments. Hair changes are generally judged over months.
quick.risks: It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, and safety data were not covered in the sources reviewed. Human trial results for this use were not found.

angle.text: Topical adenosine is used for thicker-looking hair: it acts on dermal papilla cells and lengthens the growth phase in lab studies. The research so far is in cultured cells and follicles.

procyanidin-b2.summary: An apple polyphenol used in hair-growth tonics to stimulate the follicle growth phase for more scalp hair.

quick.overview:
Procyanidin B2 is a polyphenol found in apples, used in hair-growth tonics by people wanting thicker scalp hair as a natural option.

Proposed actions include protecting hair epithelial cells from TGF-beta-induced cell death and boosting keratin expression, which supports the growth phase. Research includes cell studies, apple-extract studies in mice, and a 2018 randomized trial of an Annurca apple formulation whose extracts were rich in procyanidin B2. Most of this used extracts rather than the isolated compound.
quick.how: It is used as a topical tonic or lotion, or as an apple extract, in a regular scalp routine. Hair changes are generally judged over months.
quick.risks: Procyanidins are common in food. Safety of concentrated supplements was not assessed in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Procyanidin B2 is an apple polyphenol used to stimulate the follicle growth phase for more scalp hair. Studies include cell work, mouse work and a small human trial, mostly of whole apple extracts.

garlic-gel.summary: A folk garlic preparation applied to bald patches in alopecia areata to encourage regrowth; raw garlic on skin has caused burns.

quick.overview:
Garlic gel is a home remedy rubbed onto the scalp for alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of patchy hair loss, with the aim of regrowing hair in bald spots.

Proponents say it stimulates the scalp and may calm local immune activity, though no mechanism has been established in the sources available. The only registered trial found was a small phase 3 study of a topical garlic concentrate in children that began in 2016 and was terminated after eight participants, with no results posted.
quick.how: It is discussed in non-prescription regrowth contexts and applied as a gel or preparation to patches of hair loss. It is used alongside or instead of standard alopecia areata treatments.
quick.risks: Raw garlic applied to skin has been reported to cause burns, and references advise caution, especially in young children. It is not an approved treatment for alopecia areata.

angle.text: Garlic gel is a folk remedy applied to bald patches in alopecia areata, with the hope of regrowth in those spots. One children's trial was registered and terminated after eight participants; raw garlic has caused skin burns.

avobenzone.summary: The main organic UVA filter in US sunscreens, used to protect skin from photoageing wrinkles and dark spots; needs stabilisers in sunlight.

quick.overview:
Avobenzone is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVA light, the part of sunlight linked to photoageing. It is found in many sunscreens and SPF moisturisers, and people use it to keep skin from developing wrinkles and dark spots.

It absorbs UVA photons and releases the energy as heat, so less UV reaches skin cells. It is the main UVA-absorbing organic filter permitted in the US, at up to 3% (5% in the EU). FDA-sponsored trials in 2019 and 2020 found it is absorbed into the bloodstream after application.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily sunscreen or SPF moisturiser, reapplied through sun exposure. It breaks down in sunlight unless formulated with stabilisers such as octocrylene, so it is usually sold in blends.
quick.risks: Regulators have asked for more safety data on systemic absorption; the studies measured blood levels, not harm. Allergy and environmental concerns have been reported, and Palau banned it in 2020. It is sold over the counter.

angle.text: Avobenzone absorbs UVA light, so less photoageing damage builds up and skin stays smoother and more even over time. UVA protection is its studied purpose, and it needs stabilisers to hold up in sunlight.

octinoxate.summary: A common UVB sunscreen and lip balm filter that helps prevent sunburn and sun-driven skin aging.

quick.overview:
Octinoxate is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB, the burning part of sunlight. It is common in sunscreens, SPF lip balms and cosmetics, and people use it to avoid sunburn, uneven tone and sun-related aging.

It absorbs UVB (about 290-320 nm) and dissipates the energy as heat. Its appearance benefit comes through sun protection generally. Lab studies have reported hormone-like activity and trials show it enters the bloodstream, and in 2025 the EU's SCCS concluded it is safe up to 10%.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily sunscreen or in SPF lip balm and makeup. Sunlight can convert it to a form that absorbs less, so it is usually blended with other filters.
quick.risks: Reported concerns are endocrine activity in cell and animal studies, systemic absorption and coral reef effects; human clinical harm has not been shown in the studies listed. Hawaii and Palau restrict it. Allowed levels are 7.5% in the US and 10% in the EU.

angle.text: Octinoxate absorbs UVB light, so there is less sun damage, fewer sunspots and less wrinkling over time. Its UVB absorption is well characterised; the appearance benefit comes from sun protection generally.

oxybenzone.summary: A broad-spectrum sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB and short UVA light to help skin stay smoother and more even in the sun.

quick.overview:
Oxybenzone is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB and part of UVA light. It was long among the most common sunscreen ingredients, and people use it to limit photodamage and keep skin smoother and more even-toned.

It absorbs UV photons between about 270 and 350 nm and releases the energy as heat. It is absorbed through the skin, was detected in about 97% of US urine samples tested in 2003-2004, and is linked in lab studies to coral damage.
quick.how: It is applied in sunscreens and lip products as part of a daily or beach-day routine. Its use in US sunscreens has declined.
quick.risks: Reported issues include skin allergy, systemic absorption, endocrine activity in lab assays and coral toxicity findings. Hawaii, the US Virgin Islands, Palau, Aruba and others restrict it. The FDA lists it as lacking sufficient safety data, but it remains legal.

angle.text: Oxybenzone absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, so less photodamage accumulates and skin keeps a more even tone. The appearance case rests on sunscreen-class evidence for UV protection.

octisalate.summary: A mild UVB sunscreen ingredient that lifts SPF and keeps other filters stable so daily sunscreen protects skin from photoaging.

quick.overview:
Octisalate is a salicylate-based sunscreen ingredient that absorbs a little UVB light. Its main job is to raise SPF and help keep filters like avobenzone from breaking down, so a daily sunscreen protects skin from photoaging.

It is also an emollient that adds water resistance to formulas. It is a minor filter with less research than headline ingredients, mostly absorption and allergy studies. A 2020 JAMA trial found it enters the bloodstream.
quick.how: It is part of daily sunscreens and SPF moisturisers, where it is blended with other filters rather than used alone.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says under 1% penetrates the skin and sensitisation potential is minor. European regulators required endocrine-related testing in 2020, and it is classed as highly toxic to aquatic life in REACH registrations.

angle.text: Octisalate boosts SPF and steadies other filters, so daily sunscreen limits UV damage and slows visible skin aging. The evidence is for sunscreen formulas as a class.

homosalate.summary: A common UVB sunscreen filter used for daily sun protection that helps keep skin even-toned and younger-looking.

quick.overview:
Homosalate is a chemical sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light and is used to build SPF. It is reported in roughly 45% of US sunscreens, and people use it for daily protection against sunburn and photodamage.

Its salicylate group absorbs UVB (about 295-315 nm) and its bulky ring keeps it from washing out in water. Its appearance benefit is inferred from sunscreen-class evidence. European regulators have examined it for hormone-like effects seen in lab assays; summaries disagree on how firm the concern is.
quick.how: It is applied as part of daily sunscreen or SPF cosmetics, usually blended with other filters.
quick.risks: A 2020 trial found it is absorbed into blood after sunscreen use. Lab studies report anti-androgenic and estrogenic activity; the EU has set a concentration limit and required further testing, and it has been measured in coastal waters and coral tissue. Human harm has not been demonstrated in the studies listed.

angle.text: Homosalate absorbs UVB light, so there is less sunburn and photodamage and skin looks more even and younger over time. The appearance link comes from sunscreen-class evidence.

ensulizole.summary: A water-soluble UVB filter for light, non-greasy facial lotions so you can wear sun protection under makeup daily.

quick.overview:
Ensulizole is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs mostly UVB light. Because it dissolves in water, it appears in light lotions and daily facial moisturisers with SPF, so people can wear sun protection every day under makeup and slow sun-driven aging.

It absorbs UVB in the skin-surface layer of a product and offers little UVA protection. It is an approved US over-the-counter sunscreen active, and published research on ensulizole alone is thin, with most covering sunscreens generally.
quick.how: It is used in daily facial moisturisers and lotions with SPF, usually combined with filters such as avobenzone, zinc oxide or bemotrizinol for UVA coverage.
quick.risks: Sunscreen filters as a group can cause allergic or photoallergic reactions in some people, and labels advise stopping use if rash or irritation occurs. Environmental studies have detected PBSA in water and examined effects on fish and mussels.

angle.text: Ensulizole gives light daily facial sun protection, so there is less photoaging and uneven tone over time. Evidence is sunscreen-class, and it needs other filters for UVA coverage.

ecamsule.summary: L'Oreal's photostable UVA filter, Mexoryl SX, used in sunscreens to protect skin from UVA wrinkling and pigmentation.

quick.overview:
Ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) is a UVA-absorbing sunscreen ingredient developed by L'Oreal in the 1980s. People seek it for protection against the UVA rays linked to wrinkling and pigmentation.

It absorbs UVA light and dissipates the energy as heat while staying chemically stable in sunlight. Sunscreens containing it have been sold in Europe and Canada since 1993, and published human studies of such sunscreens report protection against UV-induced skin changes. In the US it is approved only in sunscreens registered through a New Drug Application.
quick.how: It is used in daily sunscreens and facial SPF products, usually paired with other filters because it does not cover the full UV range alone.
quick.risks: A 2019 JAMA trial found sunscreen actives including ecamsule were absorbed into plasma above the FDA's screening threshold; the authors did not conclude this meant harm. Other sources describe low systemic effects and no photomutagenicity in vitro.

angle.text: Ecamsule is a photostable UVA filter, so less UVA photoaging reaches the skin, with fewer wrinkles and dark spots over time. Appearance outcomes are inferred from UVA protection in general.

bemotrizinol.summary: A photostable broad-spectrum UV filter (Tinosorb S) long used in EU, Australian and Asian sunscreens for daily protection against skin aging.

quick.overview:
Bemotrizinol is an oil-soluble sunscreen filter that covers both UVB and UVA and is very photostable, so protection holds through the day. Skincare enthusiasts seek it out in EU, Australian and Asian products to limit photoaging and pigmentation.

It absorbs UV across about 280-400 nm, converts it to heat and helps stabilise filters like avobenzone. It has been approved in the EU since 2000. Wikipedia reports an FDA announcement of approval for US sunscreens on 9 June 2026.
quick.how: It is used in daily sunscreens, often imported or chosen from non-US brands, and blended with other filters.
quick.risks: Registered trials of a 6% sunscreen examined absorption, phototoxicity, photoallergy and irritation. Lab studies found no estrogenic activity, and aquatic toxicity studies exist.

angle.text: Bemotrizinol is a photostable UVA and UVB filter, so the sunscreen keeps working through the day and less photoaging and pigmentation builds up. Support comes from sunscreen testing and long regional use.

bisoctrizole.summary: A particle-form UV filter (Tinosorb M) that covers UVA and UVB to protect skin from sunspots and wrinkles; common abroad.

quick.overview:
Bisoctrizole is a sunscreen ingredient sold as microfine particles. It absorbs UVA and UVB and is sometimes described as a hybrid between chemical and mineral filters, sought by people who want broad coverage against photoaging.

The particles absorb UV and dissipate it as heat, and it is reported to show little photodegradation. It is approved in the EU and several other regions, but not by the US FDA. Research is mostly formulation, skin-penetration and environmental work.
quick.how: It is used in daily sunscreens, often alongside other filters, and is found mainly in products sold outside the US.
quick.risks: Sources describe minimal skin penetration and no estrogenic activity in lab tests. Environmental studies have measured it in sediment and tested aquatic species.

angle.text: Bisoctrizole is a particle filter that covers UVA and UVB, so less UV skin damage means fewer sunspots and wrinkles over time. Evidence is sunscreen-class and formulation-based.

diethylamino-hydroxybenzoyl-hexyl-benzoa.summary: A photostable UVA filter (Uvinul A Plus) common in non-US sunscreens, used to protect against UVA wrinkling and dark spots.

quick.overview:
DHHB is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVA light, the rays tied to wrinkles and dark spots. It is photostable and used in products in the EU, Japan and other markets.

It absorbs UVA near 354 nm and dissipates the energy, and studies show it interacts with other filters to help stabilise them. The EU approved it for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10%. Published work on DHHB is mostly laboratory and regulatory.
quick.how: It is used in daily sunscreens, usually blended with other filters, and is found mainly in products sold outside the US, where it is not a sunscreen active.
quick.risks: The main regulatory concern is a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate, for which EU advisers recommended strict limits. Environmental monitoring studies have detected UV filters on beaches.

angle.text: DHHB is a photostable UVA filter, so less UVA-driven damage means less wrinkling and pigmentation over time. Support comes from lab and regulatory data.

ethylhexyl-triazone.summary: A highly photostable UVB filter used in high-SPF sunscreens abroad to reach strong protection without much greasiness.

quick.overview:
Ethylhexyl triazone is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB light and is used in the EU and elsewhere to help reach high SPF values, so people can get strong protection that preserves skin tone.

It absorbs UVB near 314 nm and dissipates the energy as heat. It is described as highly photostable and is allowed in the EU at up to 5%. Sources are thin, and no clinical trials of it alone were found.
quick.how: It is used in high-SPF daily sunscreens, typically combined with UVA filters, and is found mainly in products sold outside the US.
quick.risks: Sunscreen filters as a class are recognised photoallergens in dermatology clinics. Environmental studies have measured similar filters in wastewater, sludge and sediment. It is not an approved US sunscreen active.

angle.text: Ethylhexyl triazone is a photostable UVB filter that lifts SPF without much greasiness, so less sunburn and photoaging reach the skin. The link to appearance comes from sunscreen use generally.
